title: Evaluation of urinary porphyrin excretion in neonates born to mothers exposed to airborne hexachlorobenzene.
ehr_evidence: Information on maternal history, sex, and fetal exposure to alcohol and tobacco consumption was obtained through a questionnaire prepared ad hoc for this study; we obtained 68 urine specimens of singletons neonates on the third day after birth to test for urinary porphyrin excretion, plus 52 fetal cord blood and 56 maternal serum samples for HCB analysis.
summary: A cross-sectional study of 68 full-term singleton neonates and their mothers in the HCB-exposed village of Flix and neighboring villages (Spain) examining prenatal HCB exposure (cord blood and maternal serum) and urinary porphyrin excretion.
key_findings: No positive relationship between urinary porphyrin excretion and HCB levels in cord blood or maternal serum.
Median HCB levels were 1.08 ng/mL in cord blood and 3.31 ng/mL in maternal serum; total urinary porphyrin was 37.87 µmol/mol creatinine.
Neonates in the highest tertile of HCB had lower levels of CPI and CPIII (p < 0.05).
The negative association of CPI with the highest tertile of HCB remained statistically significant after adjusting for smoking and alcohol (p < 0.05).
In neonates born to smoking mothers, total porphyrin and CPIII excretion were higher than in non-smokers (p < 0.05).
Exposed-group neonates had higher CPIII than nonexposed (p < 0.05), an association that disappeared after adjusting for smoking.
Heptaporphyrin isomer III was detected in 14 exposed cases (35.9%) versus 3 nonexposed (9.4%) (p < 0.012), all within normal range.
population: 68 full-term singleton neonates born 1997-1999 at Móra d'Ebre Hospital and their mothers, 38 from the HCB-exposed village of Flix and 30 from neighboring villages, Spain
limitations: Small sample size (n = 68) precludes firm conclusions.
Confounding by maternal smoking and alcohol consumption, which differed between exposed and nonexposed groups.
Exposure and lifestyle data obtained via ad hoc questionnaire.
Porphyrin excretion profile varies during the first days of life.
